newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan arrests ex-health official in HIV scandal.
newsitem.headline: Japan arrests ex-health official in HIV scandal.

text.p: Japan prosecutors arrested a former Health Ministry official on Friday on charges of professional negligence resulting in two deaths in a decade-old scandal involving HIV-contaminated blood products.
Akihito Matsumura, 55, who headed the ministry's Biologics and Antibiotics Division from 1984 to 1986 and is now retired, was the first government official to be arrested in the scandal.

The arrest could lead to wider investigations into the alleged role of the government in the case, in which some 400 haemophiliacs died after being given HIV-tainted products and hundreds more were infected with the virus.
Matsumura is accused of failing to order the recall of untreated blood products even though he knew unheated products could be contaminated with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS.
The two male victims, who were infected with HIV through the blood products, were a haemophiliac who died in December 1991 and a man with a liver ailment who died of AIDS last December.

The ministry approved heated blood products in July 1985 but did not order drug companies to recall unheated blood products. The unheated blood products were not fully withdrawn from the market until 1988.
In September, prosecutors arrested the then incumbent and two former presidents of Green Cross Corp on suspicion of professional negligence resulting in death.

Prosecutors last month also indicted the former head of a Health Ministry AIDS research team, Abe Takeshi, who has been under arrest since August on charges of professional negligence resulting in the death of a haemophiliac patient.

Having maintained for years it could not find documents, in February the ministry made public files from the 1983 study group Abe chaired which indicated health authorities were aware of the danger of HIV infection from unheated products.

In March, Japanese haemophiliacs accepted an out-of-court settlement in which the plaintiffs agreed to a one-time payment, putting an end to a seven-year legal battle against the state and five pharmaceutical firms.
Health Minister Naoto Kan became popular because of his pivotal role in forcing his ministry to accept responsibility for the scandal, in which about 1,800 haemophiliacs were infected with HIV.
Recent Health Ministry figures show that there are 1,154 people with AIDS and 2,942 infected with the HIV virus in Japan, a nation of 125.6 million.
